# GodotTrench

GodotTrench is a level editor for Godot in the tradition of TrenchBroom and Hammer. You block out a level from brushes, carve it with CSG, add meshes, terrain and props, and wire the gameplay together with Hammer style inputs and outputs. The editor is a standalone Rust application. A fork of FuncGodot, installed as an addon in your Godot project, turns the saved map into a real scene with meshes, collision and working entities.

This wiki holds the practical knowledge: how to set a project up, how the editor thinks, and how entities talk to each other once the map runs. The source lives at [Paraxdev/GodotTrench](https://github.com/Paraxdev/GodotTrench).

## Where to start

If you have never opened the editor, go through [[getting-started]]. It connects a Godot project to the editor and walks you through a first room, which is the quickest way to understand the round trip from brush to scene.

Once that works, the [[editor-guide]] explains how the interface is organized and which tool to reach for, and [[shortcuts]] keeps the keys in one place. [[building-in-godot]] covers what happens on the Godot side when you save: rebuilds, hot reload in a running game, streaming and the debug overlay.

Gameplay is built with entity I/O. Read [[io-concepts]] first, because everything else assumes you know what an output, a target and an activator are. After that, the [[entity-reference]] describes every entity that ships, and two worked examples, [[button-door-example]] and [[cutscene-example]], show the wiring end to end. If your game code is C#, [[csharp-entities]] explains how your own classes become placeable entities.

The **Practical uses** series builds real things from start to finish. [[terrain-painting]] explains how terrain is shaped and painted and how it comes out in Godot, and [[sea-island]] puts it to work on a large island with cliffs, a beach and paths, one screenshot per step.

## How the pieces fit

> [!NOTE] Three parts, one file format
> The **editor** writes `.gtm` map files, which are JSON. The **addon** reads them inside Godot and builds nodes. The **game config**, `godottrench_game.json`, flows the other way: the addon exports your project's entities and textures so the editor knows what it can place. When something looks wrong on one side, one of these three is usually out of date.
